chapter.title: A First Model
chapter.para: In this chapter we develop a program that can tell two kinds of points apart. We begin with a single neuron and then build, from layers of neurons, a small network that finds its own weights.

section.title: Two Kinds of Points
section.para: Let there be a plane with the coordinates x and y, each from -6 to +6. Into this plane we put points of two kinds: orange and blue. In the programs the kind of a point is represented by a number: 1 for orange and -1 for blue.

A model is a function that computes, from the coordinates x and y of a place in this plane, a guess of the kind of a point at that place: a value between -1 and +1. At -1 the model is sure that a blue point lies there; at +1 it predicts an orange one with certainty. Values in between express uncertainty: the sign says which kind the model leans to, and the nearer the value is to 0, the less sure it is; at 0 it cannot decide.
We could write such a function any way we like, for example

mediaobject.alt: The plane coloured by f(x, y) = x / 6: blue on the left, orange on the right, pale in the middle.

section.para: It is +1 at the right edge, -1 at the left and 0 on the upright axis: on the right it guesses orange, on the left blue, and the nearer the middle, the less sure it is. Or

mediaobject.alt: The plane coloured by f(x, y) = 1 − (x² + y²)/36: an orange disc in the middle, blue corners.

section.para: It is +1 at the centre, −1 in the four corners, because there x2+y2=36+36=72, and 0 on the circle of radius 6 around the centre, where x2+y2=36. Whether such a function can predict the points' kinds well depends on where they lie: the first suits points that are orange on the right and blue on the left, the second an orange disc in a blue ring.

Machine learning, on the other hand, does not make the formula up. It fixes only its general form, a formula with numbers left open, the parameters. In the second example the 36 could be such an open number, f⁡(x,y)=1−(x2+y2)/c, and c would decide how large the orange disc is; where the formula falls below −1, it counts as −1. Which values the parameters get, a program finds out from examples, points whose kind is known. Finding them is what this book calls learning, and a function with its parameters found a trained model.

sidebar.para: What an open number does, you can try for yourself: open the page with the model f⁡(x,y)=1−(x2+y2)/c and move c back and forth. The colouring follows the formula: a large c makes the orange disc large, a small one small.

section.title: One Neuron
section.para: The simplest form of such a function is a neuron. It multiplies each of its inputs by a number of its own, its weight, adds them up and adds one more number, its bias:

The result z is called the neuron's weighted sum. Where it is positive the neuron guesses orange, where it is negative, blue. The points where z is exactly 0 form a straight line, so a neuron parts the plane by a line: the weights turn it, the bias moves it.

Now let us try to adjust the neuron so that it can tell, as well as possible, the colour of six points we scatter over the plane at will: three orange and three blue. We begin with the weights 1 and 1 and the bias 0:

mediaobject.alt: The plane parted by the line x + y = 0, orange to the upper right, blue to the lower left; six points, a dark ring around an orange one on the blue side.

section.para: Five of the six lie on the right side; the one in the ring is orange but lies below the line. With w2=0 the line turns to the upright axis, and all six are right:

mediaobject.alt: The plane parted by the upright axis, orange on the right, blue on the left; all six points on the side of their colour.

section.para: Changing the weights and the bias step by step until the guesses are right is the essence of what we shall call learning.

sidebar.para: Open the page with the neuron and pull at w1, w2 and b: the line turns and moves, and the page counts how many of the six points lie right. With a click and a right click you can put down points of your own as well. Below the picture stands the function in Scaly that the page computes for it.

section.title: How Wrong
section.para: To change the weights by itself a program needs a measure of how wrong the neuron is. This measure is a number that gets smaller as the neuron gets better. Counting the wrong guesses does not serve: a small change of a weight usually changes no guess at all, so the count does not say which way to turn.
So we first map the weighted sum z to a number between −1 and 1 by a smooth function, here the hyperbolic tangent:

mediaobject.alt: The curve of tanh: near −1 on the left, rising through the origin and coming ever closer to 1 on the right; dashed, the lines at 1 and −1.

section.para: With this function the model can answer as the beginning of the chapter asked: near +1 or -1 where it is sure, near 0 where it is not. Such a function we shall call the neuron's activation function, and a its answer for a particular point of the plane. Now the answer can be compared with the kind t the point really has:

L is the loss of one point: 0 where the answer is exactly the kind, larger the further it is from it, and every small change of a weight changes it a little. The mean of the losses of all points is the neuron's loss, and that is the measure we were looking for.

The hyperbolic tangent is not the only possible activation function. In large networks one mostly takes an even simpler function today, ReLU: max⁡(0,z), that is z itself where z is positive and 0 elsewhere. Its slope is always 1 for positive z, while that of tanh becomes nearly 0 far out. What that means for learning shows in the next section.

section.title: Downhill
section.para: So the loss of our neuron is a function of the three values w1, w2 and b. Now we want to find the values for which it becomes as small as possible. Trying every combination is out of the question: each of the three values can be any number, so there are infinitely many. Even if we tried only 100 numbers for each value, that would be 1003, a million combinations, and for each we would have to compute the loss over all points. For three values a computer still manages that, but the network for XOR that we build later already has 13 numbers and so 10013=1026 combinations, and large networks have millions of weights. So we begin with some values and move from there step by step in the direction in which the loss falls fastest, with all three values at once. Which direction that is can be read off each value separately: how much does the loss change when the value changes a little? That is the partial derivative of the loss with respect to that value, for w1 written ∂L/∂w1. It is partial because only this one value changes while the others are held fixed; the round ∂ instead of a d marks that.
The loss does not depend on w1 directly. It depends on the answer a, the answer on the sum z, and the sum on w1. Each link of that chain has a derivative that is easy to work out:

listitem.para: How much does the loss change when the answer changes? ∂L∂a=a−t, the derivative of 12(a−t)2.
How much does the answer change when the sum changes? ∂a∂z=1−a2, the derivative of tanh.
How much does the sum change when w1 changes? ∂z∂w1=x, because w1 is multiplied by x.

section.para: The chain rule says that the derivative of the whole chain is the product of the derivatives of its links:

For w2 the last factor is y, for the bias it is 1. Added up over all points and divided by their number, these partial derivatives are the gradient: the direction in which the loss rises fastest. One step of gradient descent moves each of the three values a little the other way,
where the small number η is the learning rate.

And when does one stop? When the loss is small enough, or when it hardly falls any more. The pages of this chapter stop as soon as the loss is below 0.02 or has fallen by less than 0.0001 over a hundred steps. Such a rule is called a stopping criterion.

sidebar.para: Open the page where the neuron learns. It begins with values that guess badly: only two of the six points are right. Press “One step” several times in a row: w1, w2 and b move a bit each time, the line turns, the loss falls. Press “Learn”: after some thirty steps all six are right; after a good eighty the loss is below 0.02, and learning stops. w2 is then nearly 0, as in our attempt by hand. With the learning rate 0.01 it goes much more slowly. Below the picture stands the step in Scaly.

section.para: Try the start values w1=w2=−3 as well (the page with these values): then the neuron hardly moves, and after a hundred steps the page stops, since the loss no longer falls. Nearly all points lie on the wrong side, and far from the line, where tanh is nearly ±1 and hardly rises any more. Since the factor 1−a2 is nearly 0 there, so is the gradient: a neuron that is sure and wrong hardly learns. This is called saturation, and it is why one begins with small weights.

section.title: Better Inputs
section.para: Our neuron parts the plane by a line. But some arrangements of points cannot be parted by a line, for example a disc of orange points inside a ring of blue ones: every line then has orange and blue on both sides.

sidebar.para: Open the page where the neuron learns and put down unfavourable points yourself: some orange ones in the middle and a ring of blue ones around them. A click puts down an orange point, a right click a blue one, a click on a point takes it away. Press “Learn”: the neuron finds no line that fits, settles for a plane that is unsure everywhere, and stops, since the loss no longer falls.

section.para: What the neuron lacks is not skill at sums but the right view of the points. Let us give it the squares of x and y as its inputs instead:
With w1=w2=−1 and b=9, say, z is 0 exactly where x2+y2=9, on the circle of radius 3 around the centre. Inside, z is positive, outside negative:

mediaobject.alt: The plane with an orange circle of radius 3 around the centre, blue elsewhere; the orange points of the disc lie inside the circle, the blue ones of the ring outside.

section.para: Why can the neuron do this all of a sudden? Let us call its new inputs u=x2 and v=y2. Then z=w1u+w2v+b is a straight line again, only not in the plane of x and y but in that of u and v. Drawn there, the disc lies near the origin and the ring further out, and a line parts them:

mediaobject.alt: The same points over u = x² and v = y²: the orange ones near the origin below a slanting line, the blue ones further out above it.

section.para: So the neuron still draws a line, but a line in the inputs it is given; on the plane of the points it becomes a circle. Choosing what a model sees is called feature engineering, and good inputs can make a hard problem easy.

sidebar.para: Open the page with the neuron given x² and y². It begins with the disc and the ring and guesses badly at first. Press “Learn”: after some hundred steps all points are right, and the orange area settles around the disc; after a good two hundred the loss is below 0.02. Here too you can put down points and take them away.

section.title: Hidden Layers
section.para: For a disc the right inputs are easy to guess; for most data they are not. So we leave it to neurons to compute the inputs. It is this idea that makes neural networks strong.

Let us take several neurons instead of one. Each of them is given the same inputs x and y, but has weights and a bias of its own and so draws a line of its own; its answer says on which side of it a point lies. Neurons that read the same inputs like this form a layer. Now we form one more layer. It is given not x and y but the answers of the neurons of the first layer, and here it consists of a single neuron, the output. So the computation runs in two stages: from x and y the first layer computes its answers, and from those answers the output computes its own. From outside one sees only the inputs and the output, so the layer in between is called a hidden layer; its answers are intermediate results.

The data that shows it best is called XOR: orange at the upper right and the lower left, blue at the other two corners. No single line parts them. Two neurons in a hidden layer can, if each cuts off one of the orange corners. Let their answer here simply be the sign sgn of their weighted sum, +1 or −1. The first says +1 only at the upper right:

mediaobject.alt: The plane with the points of XOR, orange only beyond the line x + y = 3 at the upper right, blue elsewhere.

section.para: the second only at the lower left:

mediaobject.alt: The plane with the points of XOR, orange only beyond the line x + y = −3 at the lower left, blue elsewhere.

section.para: The output reads the two answers. If either of them says +1, z=h1+h2+1 is +1, so orange; if both say −1, it is −1, so blue:

mediaobject.alt: The plane with the points of XOR: orange at the upper right and lower left corners, a blue band between them; every point on the side of its colour.

section.para: How the output manages that shows when each point is put where the hidden layer takes it. The output is a neuron like our first one, only its inputs are called h1 and h2 instead of x and y. So it does not see the plane of the points but a new plane with the axes h1 and h2, and in it each point has the place (h1,h2): the three orange points at the upper right land at (+1,−1), the three at the lower left at (−1,+1), and all six blue ones at (−1,−1). In this plane a single line parts the two kinds, and that line is the one the output draws:

mediaobject.alt: The plane of the answers h1 and h2: an orange point at (+1, −1), one at (−1, +1), a blue one at (−1, −1); the line h1 + h2 + 1 = 0 parts the blue one at the lower left from the orange ones.

section.para: The output joins the two lines into an or: orange where the first or the second neuron says yes. Two lines and a neuron that joins them do what one line alone cannot. With more neurons and more layers, borders of any intricacy can be built this way.

sidebar.para: Open the page with a network of one hidden layer. It has three hidden neurons and begins on the points of XOR with small weights that guess only half of the points right. Press “Learn”: after a good hundred steps all twelve are right. The small pictures show which line each hidden neuron has found; the output joins them. Further down the page the network stands in layers, one above the other, with the weights as lines; drag it with the mouse to turn it. How the network finds its thirteen numbers is the next section’s subject.

section.para: The activation function matters here. If each neuron simply passed on its weighted sum, the output would add up sums of sums, which is again only a weighted sum of x and y, so again only a line. Only the activation function, which bends each neuron's sum, lets the layers do more than one neuron could. In our example by hand that is the sign; in the network from the box above, the hyperbolic tangent.

section.title: Backpropagation
section.para: How does a hidden neuron learn? Its weights are as far from the loss as can be, behind the output neuron. The chain rule still works, with a chain one link longer. The clever part is the order in which it is computed.

First everything is computed forward, as before: each hidden neuron's answer hj, then the output's sum and its answer a. Then backward. The output neuron's share of the error, the loss by its sum, is the familiar

and its weights' derivatives follow from it as for a single neuron: dhj for the weight vj that reads hidden neuron j. Hidden neuron j reaches the loss through that weight, so its answer's slope is dvj, and through its own tanh its share of the error becomes

From there its weights are once more a single neuron's: djx, djy and dj for its bias. The error is handed back through the network layer by layer, each layer's share computed from the share of the layer after it. That is backpropagation, and it is the whole secret of how networks of any depth learn.

sidebar.para: Open the page with the network for XOR once more. Below the picture there is now the procedure network_step: backpropagation as derived here. For each point it computes forward the answers hj and a, then back d and from it each dj, and at the end it moves each of the thirteen numbers a little against its gradient. Each press of One step is one call of this procedure.

section.para: The hidden neurons on the page start from different weights on purpose. Had they all started alike, they would answer alike, get the same gradient in every step and stay alike forever, three copies of one line. That is why a network usually starts from random weights.
A network needs nothing more to learn, however many layers it has: compute forward, hand the error back, move each weight a little against its gradient.

section.title: The Field
section.para: The networks in our boxes were small and each built for one task. The field is a page on which you put a network together yourself and watch it learn. You choose the points, the inputs, how many hidden layers it has and how many neurons in each, and how it learns. It computes exactly as the last sections derived. At the top of the page lies a bar with the buttons. Below it stand three parts side by side, from left to right the data, the network and the output; on a narrow screen they stand one below the other. The picture shows the page with the spiral, after a little over 2000 steps; a click on it shows it at full size.

mediaobject.alt: The field: at the top the bar with Pause, One step, Start again, the count of the steps, learning rate, activation function, regularization and speed; below it on the left the data with the spiral chosen, in the middle the network with the seven inputs, two hidden layers of six and four neurons and the output, on the right the two losses, their course and the plane with the points of the spiral.

listitem.para: Pause stops the network; the same button is then called Learn and lets it learn on. While it is stopped, One step takes exactly one step of gradient descent over all the training points. Start again gives the network new random weights and keeps the points. Beside them the page counts the steps since the start.

The Learning rate is the one from the section “Downhill”, to choose from 0.001 to 3. Under Activation function there are four to choose from, for the neurons of the hidden layers: the hyperbolic tangent, ReLU, the sigmoid function σ⁡(z)=11+e−z, which runs between 0 and 1 instead of between −1 and +1, and none. Without an activation function each hidden neuron simply hands on its weighted sum, and the whole network, however many layers it has, draws only one line. The output neuron always answers with the hyperbolic tangent. Regularization (L2) is explained in the next section.
The Speed says how many steps the network takes between two pictures, in five levels from 1 to 100. The page draws a picture every 30 milliseconds at most.

Five small pictures choose the points: Circle, a disc inside a ring; XOR, the four quarters of the plane, the kind by the sign of xy; Clouds, two heaps around (2,2) and (−2,−2); Spiral, two arms wound into each other; and Your own, an empty plane. Into it you put points yourself, an orange one with a click, a blue one with a shift-click or a right-click. For the other four the page draws 300 points, half of each kind.

The Noise slider moves each point at random, up to 50 %, so that the kinds reach into each other; for the clouds it makes the heaps wider instead. New points draws the same arrangement anew. A change of data only exchanges the points; the network learns on with the weights it has.

The network stands in columns, from left to right in the order in which it is computed. The first column holds the seven possible inputs: x, y, x2, y2, xy, sin⁡x and sin⁡y. You know the squares from the section “Better Inputs”; new are the sines of the two coordinates, which go up and down a little less than twice across the plane. A click on an input gives it to the network or takes it away. One taken away is pale and struck through, and one always stays.

Then come the hidden layers, each a column. With − and + above the network you take a layer away or add one, up to six; with − and + above a column, a neuron of that layer, up to eight. Without a hidden layer the network is a single neuron as at the beginning of the chapter. The last column is the output neuron.

Each neuron, each input too, is a small square. It shows what the neuron answers over the whole plane, orange where the answer is positive, blue where it is negative, like our pictures for XOR. The lines between the squares are the weights: orange positive, blue negative, the thicker, the larger their size. On each line a light runs from left to right, the faster, the stronger the weight. When the network's shape, its inputs or its activation function change, it starts over from new random weights.

At the top stand two numbers, the Training loss and the Test loss, below them their course since the last start: the training loss solid, the test loss dashed. What test points are is explained in the next section.

The large picture is the plane, from −6 to 6 both ways, with all the points. Beneath them lies the output neuron's answer at every place, the stronger the colour, the nearer to +1 or −1. Only the decision shows instead only on which side of zero the answer lies, and with it the border the network draws. Show the test points shows and hides the ringed points.

section.para: Below the three parts the page says in a few sentences what happens, and at the very bottom the program can be unfolded that the last section of this chapter is about. The links in the boxes set the page up to fit. What they choose stands in the address after the #. Without such settings the page starts with the circle, the inputs x and y and two hidden layers of four and two neurons.

sidebar.para: Open the field with the spiral, only x and y as inputs and one hidden layer of four neurons. The network starts learning at once, but its loss falls only slowly and stays high: four lines are not enough for the spiral. Then click sin x and sin y in the column of the inputs. The network starts again, and after a few seconds its loss has fallen to a fraction.

section.title: Generalization
section.para: A model that knows its training points is not yet useful. The question is how well it guesses points it has never seen. That is why the field holds back half of its points as test points, drawn with a ring: the network never learns from them, and the loss over them, the test loss, says how well it generalizes.

When the data is noisy and the network large, the two losses part ways. The network learns the training points ever better, noise included, and draws borders around single stray points; the test loss stops falling and rises. That is overfitting. One cure is regularization: an extra loss for large weights, λw2 for each weight. Its derivative shrinks every weight a little in every step, and a network with smaller weights draws smoother borders.

sidebar.para: Open the spiral with 30 % noise and four hidden layers of eight. After some seconds the training loss is far below the test loss, and the plane shows islands around single points. Choose 0.01 under Regularization (L2) and Start again: the training loss stays higher, the test loss ends lower, the borders are smoother.

section.title: The Field's Program
section.para: The page runs one Scaly program, field.scaly, built for WebAssembly. It is this chapter's programs grown up: everything the page lets you set, and backpropagation as in the section “Backpropagation”, only in loops over layers instead of written out. It keeps everything the page shows in one vector of numbers in its memory, which the page reads directly, without a copy; the picture of the network's answer over the plane is a for over its 6400 points, which Scaly spreads over the cores of the machine by itself. Its source is on GitHub.

Everything this chapter derived by hand, the chain rule through every link and the gradient of every weight, a program can derive too. That is the subject of the chapters ahead: first how Scaly holds many numbers at once, in tensors, then a tape that records the forward computation and plays it back to get every derivative.
